name: Lemon Yellow
lede: Lemon yellow is a bright, cool yellow named for the fruit, and as a paint it was a family of nineteenth-century chromium and cadmium pigments sold under one name.

sections.title: A fruit, then a pigment
sections.body:
The swatch is a bright, slightly greenish yellow, named for the rind of the lemon. Our library places it in the ISCC-NBS block called brilliant greenish yellow, 4.0 units away on the CIEDE2000 scale [18]. The sources that carry the name run from Werner's 1821 chart through Ridgway's plates of 1886 and 1912 to the ISCC-NBS charts of 1955 [18]. The old plates, scanned after a century or more of aging, show a duller, more golden yellow than the screen swatch does [18].

As a word, "lemon yellow" was an artist's term before it was a general one, and a pigment sold under that name could have many different compositions [1][2]. Close neighbors are [[sulphur-yellow]], [[primrose-yellow]] and [[barium-yellow]], and the lemon-colored cadmium, [[cadmium-lemon]]. Each is a pale, cool yellow reached by a different route [1][9][18].

sections.title: Yellow from the metal chromium
sections.body:
The story of the pigment begins with a mineral from Siberia [1]. The chemist Vauquelin found a new metal in it and named it chromium, from the Greek for color, because its compounds came in so many hues [1]. Synthesizing pure lead chromate, he got a rich yellow; in 1804 he and Berthollet suggested it as a pigment, and by 1809, when he published his full study, chrome yellow was already on artists' palettes [1]. One early appearance is in a portrait by Thomas Lawrence dated 1810 [1].

The shade could be steered. Precipitating lead chromate together with lead sulphate gave a primrose yellow when the two were in equal parts, and a lemon yellow when the mixture held 65 per cent lead chromate; more chromate made the color deeper [1]. Vauquelin also found that adding acid to the solution gave a deep lemon yellow, which he reported as the shade painters prized most [1]. Precipitating from an alkaline solution gave orange instead, and chrome orange became the first pure, strong orange that painters had ever had [1].

Cost held the pigment back at first. While the only chromium came from remote Siberia, even Russian artists paid dearly for lead chromate, as a French dictionary of 1818 remarked [1]. Deposits of chromite found soon afterward changed that [1].

sections.title: Not one pigment but a family
sections.body:
Ask what "lemon yellow" meant in a color merchant's catalog and the answer is: it depends. Ball lists lead chromate, lead chromate with lead sulphate, and the chromates of barium and strontium, more rarely calcium [1]. The *Pigment Compendium* agrees that the term was applied variably, to barium, strontium, zinc and, less often, lead chromates [2]. It adds that in nineteenth-century British sources the name could also cover platina yellow and zinc chromate [2].

Barium chromate, described by Vauquelin in 1809, was also called yellow ultramarine, *outremer jaune* in French [1][3]. It is less opaque than lead chromate but more stable, and chrome yellow's habit of browning drew complaints as the century went on [1]. Jarman, in his notes on the yellows, remembers barium yellow and lemon yellow as stable in light and as dating from the early nineteenth century [7].

Who first used the name is only partly settled. The *Pigment Compendium* reports Harley's statement that the British colorman Field used it as a color name by the early nineteenth century, though the composition was not recorded then [2]. A modern oddity: the same book cites a paint bought in 1985 and labelled lemon yellow that proved to contain an azo pigment, not a chromate [2]. The label has never reliably told you what was in the tube [2].

sections.title: The colorman's primary yellow
sections.body:
George Field, the London colorman, gave lemon yellow a special place [1]. He held to the trinity of red, yellow and blue and set out to make a pigment for each: lemon yellow (or at an earlier point Indian yellow) for the yellow, red madder for the red and ultramarine for the blue [1]. That red-yellow-blue set is a teaching convention, not a fact of color: no three pigments mix every color, and Field's choice was a pigment maker's choice [1].

There is an older use of the word. Gage reports that Newton's Cambridge lectures of 1669-70 listed lemon yellow, in English translation, between red lead and golden yellow, in a list of eleven steps that Newton later cut to seven [6]. That shows the color word in use, not the pigment [6].

sections.title: In painting: the new yellows
sections.body:
Lemon yellow is a signature of nineteenth-century color. Ball counts twelve synthetics among the twenty principal pigments identified in Impressionist pictures, and lemon yellow (barium chromate) leads that list [4]. Renoir's *Boating on the Seine*, of 1879-80, is built from seven pigments besides lead white, one of them a lemon yellow that Ball identifies as strontium chromate [4]. So the analyses give barium in one list and strontium in another; the label covered both [4].

In a letter that Pastoureau quotes, [[painter:vincent-van-gogh|Van Gogh]] describes his *Night Café* as blood-red walls, a green billiard table and four lemon-yellow lamps radiating orange and green [15]. Here the yellow is a light, a cold sharp point among the reds and greens [15].

The chromium yellows aged less well than their makers hoped. Ball notes that chrome yellow was prone to turn brown, and he asks how anyone can tell that a patch which now looks like yellow ochre was once a brilliant lemon yellow [1][19]. His answer is chemical analysis, not the eye [19].

sections.title: Cadmium, coal tar and a berry
sections.body:
Cadmium gave the lemon shade a longer life. The metal was discovered in 1817, but commercial cadmium yellow had to wait until 1840 because the ore was scarce [9]. Its shades run from a lemon yellow through a strong primary yellow to orange, and Coles ties the shade to the grain size produced in manufacture [9].

Coal-tar lemon yellows were less fortunate. In Ball's retelling of Doerner's account, they were marketed as brighter and more permanent than the chrome and cadmium yellows and turned out to be the opposite [8]. A better class of synthetic yellow arrived in 1911 with the Hansa pigments, and Hansa Yellow G proved very lightfast [8].

A lemon-yellow lake can also come from a plant. Coles reports that buckthorn berries give a lemon-yellow lake when the dye bath is held at 50 degrees Celsius, and an orange one at 100 [10]. The shade has been reached by metal, by coal tar and by berry [8][9][10].

sections.title: The word in older hands
sections.body:
Heraldry shows how loose the color once was. The golden French lilies of the royal arms could be painted lemon yellow, orange yellow or gilded, and Pastoureau stresses that the choice carried no meaning [13]. In the seventeenth century, painters gained Naples yellow, previously used only in pyrotechnics, which supplied tones from yellow ochre to lemon yellow [14].

Werner-style lists treated lemon as one rung of a yellow ladder. Lenz's lists of color names put it between sulphur yellow and gold yellow, with straw yellow nearby [16]. Syme's recipes used lemon yellow as an ingredient: a little in grass green, some in pistachio green, a touch in a white [16].

sections.title: Myths: lemon yellow as medicine
sections.body: The claim that lemon yellow relieves heartburn comes from the old color-therapy literature, which Birren sets out as a collection of "turgid" and esoteric traditions before turning to modern thinking [12]. It is a myth, not a finding: no color heals by itself, and the line is a record of what people once believed [12]. A different medical use of the word is purely descriptive, as when a physician described the skin in pernicious anemia as a peculiar lemon-yellow tint [12].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Lemon yellow barely appears in our painting archive. Counting a painting only when the color covers at least 1 per cent of the canvas, within a CIEDE2000 distance of 4, it appears in 3 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed [19]. That is rarer than 79 per cent of the named colors [19]. The earliest of the three is a Gauguin of 1893 and the latest a Mondrian of 1922 [19]. At a stricter 5 per cent cover and a distance of 6, only one painting remains, Mondrian's [[painting:commons-Q17491107|Composition in Red, Yellow and Blue]] [19].

The count describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings: a color match is not a pigment test [19]. The screen swatch is also brighter than the old plates that carry the name [18].

Two near-namesakes are different colors. Crayola's [[lemon-yellow-crayola]] is a paler, lighter yellow than this swatch, and [[lemon-meringue]] is a creamy tint that borrows the fruit's name [18].
